title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Chicago: Scale Routing ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra on a Chicago-style grid: it launches two Dijkstra searches—one from the start, one from the goal—and meets in the middle. This visualization shows how modern route planning engines reduce work while still guaranteeing the shortest path.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡ — two searches, one meeting point.

On our Chicago (Loop) grid, we run Dijkstra forward from the start and backward from the destination simultaneously. Each frontier expands by smallest known distance, and when the best combined path stops improving, the algorithms “converge” to the shortest route.

Why this scales: instead of exploring the whole map, you roughly cut the explored space and focus computation where the paths are most likely to meet. The result: faster shortest-path at scale—exactly what a route planning engine needs.

Takeaway: Bidirectional Dijkstra is a graph-search speedup that keeps correctness, but only shines when the start/goal are meaningful and the graph is large.

Debate question: If your network is dynamic (traffic changes constantly), would you still prefer Bidirectional Dijkstra over A* with heuristics?
